rejected.title: Japan's social order
card: Under the Tokugawa shoguns, who ruled from 1603, society was ranked in fixed classes. Your class was set by birth, and it was hard to move out of it.
Top
the emperor and the court nobles sat above the four main classes. The samurai, the warrior class, ranked highest of the four.
Below the samurai
peasants came next, then craftworkers, then merchants. Peasants ranked high because they grew the rice and other food the country needed.
Merchants were the lowest of the four main classes, even when rich, because rank was about a class's role, not its wealth. Outcast groups were placed below and outside all four classes.
rejected.remember: The four main classes ran samurai, peasants, craftworkers, merchants, set by birth and role, not wealth.

a.q: Which list shows the four main classes under the Tokugawa shoguns, from highest to lowest?
opts: Samurai, peasants, craftworkers, merchants
Samurai, merchants, craftworkers, peasants
Merchants, samurai, peasants, craftworkers
Peasants, samurai, craftworkers, merchants
a.why: Samurai ranked highest of the four main classes, then peasants, craftworkers and merchants. The list with merchants second is tempting because some merchants were wealthy, but wealth did not decide rank.
a.clue: The class that traded goods was lowest of the four.

b.q: Daichi is a merchant in a Japanese town under the Tokugawa shoguns. He is richer than most samurai he knows. Where does he rank?
opts: In the lowest main class, below peasants and craftworkers
Above peasants, because his wealth gives him status
Level with samurai, because he has as much money
Above craftworkers, because he can pay for their goods
b.why: Rank was set by birth and a class's role, not by wealth. Merchants stayed in the lowest of the four main classes even when rich. The idea that money raised his rank above peasants is tempting, but it does not fit this order.
b.clue: Ask what decided rank: money or role.

draft.title: Japan's social order
card: Under the shoguns, Japanese society was ranked in classes. Where you were born decided your class, and it was hard to move out of it.
Top
the emperor and the court nobles sat above everyone. Below them, the samurai were the warrior class, and they ranked highest of the main classes.
Below the samurai
peasants came next, then craftworkers, then merchants. Peasants grew the rice and other food that the whole country needed.
Merchants ranked last, even though some became rich. The ranking was about the role a class played in society, not about how much money it had.
draft.remember: The order was samurai, peasants, craftworkers, then merchants, set by birth and role, not wealth.

a.why: Samurai ranked highest of the main classes, then peasants, craftworkers and merchants. The list with merchants second is tempting because merchants could be wealthy, but wealth did not decide rank.
a.clue: The class that traded goods ranked last.

b.q: Daichi is a merchant in a Japanese port town. He is richer than most samurai he knows. Where does he rank in the social order under the shoguns?
opts: Below peasants and craftworkers, in the lowest class
Above peasants, because his wealth gives him status
Level with samurai, because he has as much money
Above craftworkers, because he can pay for goods
b.why: Rank was set by a class's role and birth, not by wealth. Merchants stayed in the lowest of the main classes even when rich. The belief that money raised rank is tempting but does not fit this order.
b.clue: Ask what decided rank: money or role.

b.best: Below peasants and craftworkers, in the lowest class

problems.detail: The card says merchants 'ranked last' without saying 'of the main classes'. Outcast groups (eta and hinin) ranked below merchants, outside the four classes, so a student could wrongly learn that merchants were the bottom of all society.

The right option says merchants were 'in the lowest class'. That repeats the card's overstatement, because outcast groups ranked lower. 'In the lowest of the main classes' would match the why and be accurate.

The fixed four-class ranking set by birth is really the Tokugawa-era system (made firmer from Hideyoshi's time). The card applies it to all of 'under the shoguns' since 1192, which is broader than the evidence supports.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. The rigid birth-based system also belongs mainly to the Tokugawa period, not all shogunate rule.
